transcript_text:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-08-21
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 46 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Ruth Morgan (CTO, Archipelago), Ibrahim Khan (ML Eng), Sofia Lee (Product)

Summary: Quick demo/walkthrough of Redwood JSON-mode (structured output + tool calling), Console flows for onboarding a pilot, and Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization. Customer emphasized low-latency agent use case and strict data residency for logs.

Topics: JSON mode overview; schema enforcement and graceful fallback; tool routing (region/cost/latency policies); Console pilot flows; security (VPC, KMS, SOC2/ISO); Optimize cost suggestions (batching, KV cache, quantization).

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Okay everyone, thanks for joining, i'm Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account. quick roll call?
[00:08] Ruth: Ruth here, hi thanks for doing this, i'll hand off to Ibrahim and Sofia shortly.
[00:12] Ibrahim: Ibrahim, ML, hi.
[00:14] Sofia: Sofia, PM, hi all.
[00:17] Liam: Liam Patel, solutions eng, i'll run through the demo bits and the console.
[00:22] Maya: Great. Quick agenda — 20 min demo of JSON-mode + tool routing, then 15 min on console/pilot ops, and final 10 min for questions and next steps. Does that work?
[00:33] Ruth: Yep that's perfect. We're short on time so if you can hit the latency parts earlier that'd be great.
[00:38] Maya: For sure. Liam take it away.

[01:02] Liam: Cool, so first slide — JSON-mode is our structured output mode where you can provide a schema, we validate and produce typed responses. we also support tool calling / function-style invokes that return typed payloads which the runtime then dispatches. i'll share my screen here — bear with me a sec —
[01:20] [screen-sharing starts, soft click sounds] 
[01:26] Liam: Alright, in the Console you can create a contract — json schema or openapi-like spec — you can attach fallback policies; that's important for your agent workflow, because you might want graceful degradation to a free-text fallback if the model can't produce strict schema.
[01:46] Ibrahim: quick q — can the fallback be an alternate model or do you only allow free-text fallback?
[01:51] Liam: Good question. You can chain fallbacks: alternate model variants (e.g., smaller quantized for cost), or free-text. You can also route to a different infra region if latency constraints can't be met in primary region.
[02:03] Sofia: Does that mean we can prefer a low-latency region for production but fall back to a lower-cost region for batch jobs?
[02:09] Liam: Exactly — routing policy can be by latency SLO, cost threshold, or explicit allowed regions. We'll show the policy UI in the Console.

[02:30] [03:00] Maya: I want to highlight the 'typed actions' approach — your agent can ask Redwood to call a tool, for example our webhook connector or your internal action endpoint. Redwood enforces the schema, validates types, and returns structured payloads to your orchestrator. That prevents the 'stringy-parse' step you get with free-text outputs.
[03:22] Ruth: Our concern is safety — what if the model hallucinates a dangerous command or tries to leak secrets?
[03:29] Liam: We have multiple guardrails: schema validation, allowlists/denylists for actions, circuit-breakers in the runtime, and an execution sandbox for tools. Also audit logs and KMS integration for any keys used during tool invocation.
[03:45] Ibrahim: How do you handle KV cache warming for agent use-cases? we have very dynamic context windows.
[03:52] Liam: The runtime exposes prefix caching and incremental KV-resume so repeated prompts with the same state benefit from cached KV blocks. For very dynamic contexts we recommend a hybrid: small prefix + context window + partial cache hits to keep latency down.

[04:20] [04:40] Sofia: Walk me through a real example — say our agent wants to place a trade through internal API, what's the flow?
[04:47] Liam: Good one. Agent sends high-level intent -> Redwood model produces typed action per schema e.g. {action: "place_order", symbol: "ABC", qty: 100} -> Redwood validates schema -> runtime checks policies (is action allowed?) -> if allowed, the tool adapter posts to your internal API (the adapter can run in VPC or via webhook) -> adapter returns structured success/failure -> Redwood logs event in audit log and returns model + tool output to your caller.
[05:22] Ruth: you mentioned the adapter can run in our VPC — we need that for compliance.
[05:27] Liam: Yep, we support Private deployments and VPC connectors. The adapter (tool runner) can be deployed inside your VPC or we can use a customer-managed bridge. For air-gapped/strict environments we also have an on-prem option.
[05:39] Ibrahim: latency — what's the typical in-region p50/p95 for a typed action invoke?
[05:44] Liam: On hosted with our verified models, p50 is sub-80 ms for short sequences; p95 varies with sequence length — around 250-350ms depending on token count. Dedicated pools bring p95 down, and we can optimize with quantized variants and smaller sequence-length kernels.
[06:05] Ruth: Those numbers are good. We're aiming for <150ms p95 for interactive agents.
[06:10] Liam: For that SLO, we often recommend Dedicated + KV cache + aggressive batching config tuned for your QPS profile — we'll propose a config in the pilot.

[06:30] [06:55] Maya: Quick detour to 'Optimize' — this is our cost and perf suggestions engine. you upload traces or connect to the Console, it suggests batching windows, quantization level, and which model variants to use per workload. it can also recommend when to memoize responses or use prefix caching.
[07:12] Ibrahim: will Optimize give us token-level cost estimates per route?
[07:16] Maya: Yes, and it ties back to your Console routes so you can preview unit economics per policy — very helpful when trading latency vs cost.

[07:35] Liam: i'll demo the Console now — creating a schema, attaching a tool, and creating a routing policy.
[07:42] [screen content: Console UI, JSON editor view] 
[07:48] Liam: here's a sample schema we prepared for "order placement": required fields, enums for instrument types, numeric constraints for qty. you can toggle strict vs permissive validation. if strict and model output doesn't match, you can auto-invoke a recovery prompt or run a second model pass.
[08:10] Sofia: can the schema include runtime constraints, like maximum allowed qty?
[08:14] Liam: Yes you can include business rules and map them to policy checks. We support validation hooks that call your rule service before executing the tool.

[08:40] [09:00] Ibrahim: on the tool adapter — what's the auth pattern? do you manage tokens?
[09:05] Liam: Options: Redwood-managed secrets (encrypted with customer KMS) or you bring your own via a VPC adapter where credentials never leave your network. All calls are logged and can be redacted in logs per your retention policy.
[09:20] Ruth: We need SSO and RBAC including least-privilege for who can create/modify schemas and policies.
[09:27] Maya: Console supports role-based access (Admin, Operator, Viewer) and SSO via SAML/Okta; changes to policies are auditable.

[09:46] [10:12] Liam: Now i'll show tool-routing: here i create a route that prefers region "us-west" for latency, fallback to "us-east" only if p95>200ms or queue depth exceeds threshold. I can also set cost budget so if monthly spend for that route exceeds X, we'll shift to a cheaper quantized model pool.
[10:34] Sofia: that's helpful. Do we get alerts when fallback triggers?
[10:38] Liam: Yes, Console emits alerts and you can wire them to Slack or PagerDuty. We also have traces per request so you can see which rule caused routing decisions.

[10:55] [11:20] Maya: i'm going to hit a few common questions from other customers — how do you test schema changes without breaking production?
[11:27] Liam: Canary rollouts. You can point a small percent of traffic to a new schema variant and run it in "analysis mode" where we log diffs but don't surface failures to end-users until you promote.
[11:38] Ibrahim: what's the onboarding timeline for a pilot? we have internal procurement constraints.
[11:42] Maya: Typical pilot is 4–6 weeks: infra review + sample traces (week 1), pilot deploy and baseline (week 2), tuning with Optimize recommendations (weeks 3–4), then decision. We can compress if you have sample traces ready.

[12:05] [12:30] Ruth: a couple of procurement/security asks — do you have SOC 2 Type II and ISO attestations? also can we get a data processing addendum with clear data residency?
[12:40] Maya: We have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001, and we provide a DPA. For residency we can provision in a specific region or do Private deployment so logs never leave your VPC.
[12:56] Sofia: are audit logs immutable?
[13:00] Liam: They are append-only in the system; for Private you can push them to your SIEM. We also support cryptographic signing for critical events if you need stronger non-repudiation.

[13:25] [13:50] Ibrahim: small nit — transcription seems to conflate some product names in your docs, can we have a one-pager mapping console terms to api fields?
[13:58] Maya: Totally, we'll include a "field map" cheat sheet in the pilot docs.

[14:10] Liam: Quick demo of runtime logs — here's a typed action request trace: you can see request latency, which model served it, the schema validation result, and the exact tool payload. There are buttons to re-run a request in sandbox mode.
[14:31] Ruth: can we redact PII from logs automatically?
[14:35] Liam: Yes we have automatic PII redaction pipelines and you can add custom redaction rules. For guarded environments we recommend redacting at ingest in the VPC adapter.

[15:00] [15:30] Sofia: About cost — if we push many small requests (high qps small context) vs fewer large requests, what levers should we use?
[15:39] Liam: For many small requests, batching and short-circuit caching reduce per-token cost. Use continuous batching windows and optimize batching window size via Optimize. For fewer large requests, use quantized model variants and larger context optimizations. We'll model both in the cost preview.

[16:12] Maya: Alright i'm going to show the pilot doc we typically use — scope, success criteria, measurement plan (latency, correctness, cost), and rollback conditions.
[16:23] [screen shows pilot doc] 
[16:30] Maya: Success criteria you mentioned earlier: p95 < 150ms and correct schema enforcement > 99% for critical actions. Is that right?
[16:38] Ruth: that's right, and we also want less than 0.1% failed/unsafe tool invocations.
[16:43] Liam: We can instrument safety monitors to catch unsafe patterns during pilot.

[17:05] [17:30] Ibrahim: For our test data — if we share sensitive traces, what's the retention policy during pilot?
[17:36] Maya: By default we retain logs for 90 days, but for pilots we can set custom retention, and for Private deployments logs stay in your environment. We'll sign an NDA and handle traces per the DPA.

[18:00] [18:20] Sofia: can you show the API call that returns structured payloads?
[18:25] Liam: Sure — i'll paste from the Console. Example snippet: POST /v1/generate with body {"mode":"json","schema_id":"order-v1","input":"Buy 100 shares..."} response is 200 with {"result":{"action":"place_order","symbol":"ABC","qty":100},"tool_run":{"status":"ok","http_status":200}} — note responses include schema validation status and model confidence metadata.
[18:58] Ibrahim: model confidence metadata — is that calibrated?
[19:01] Liam: We provide a confidence score from the model and an internal calibration layer that looks at schema conformance and token-level logits for anomaly detection. It's not perfect but it helps triage.

[19:25] [19:45] Ruth: How do we limit which teams can create new tool connectors? We don't want developers spinning up unsafe integrations.
[19:52] Maya: RBAC plus approval workflows. Creating a connector requires operator-level rights and we can enforce code review of adapter templates.

[20:10] [20:35] Liam: Quick mention of fallback orchestration — if schema validation fails twice, we can escalate to a human-in-the-loop flow, open a ticket, or route to a safe sandbox. You can compose these in the Console visually.
[20:52] Sofia: nice. will that add to latency?
[20:55] Liam: The orchestration step is additional but you can control when it's triggered. For mission-critical flows we prefer preventing unsafe actions even at the cost of extra latency.

[21:20] [21:40] Maya: We're nearing the end; any other blockers or stick points from your side?
[21:45] Ruth: procurement needs clarity on pricing for Dedicated pools and SLA terms.
[21:51] Maya: We'll include detailed pricing tiers in the pilot proposal. Dedicated often requires a commit for predictable throughput; we'll show a few options.

[22:10] [22:30] Ibrahim: last technical Q — do you support ONNX or custom kernels for certain models? we might want to bring a specialized model later.
[22:39] Liam: We support common model formats and can onboard custom weights — kernel selection is automatic but we can work with you on a test to ensure peak perf. For private deployments we can include your custom runtime.

[23:00] [23:20] Sofia: Is there a throttling policy we can set per-tenant inside our account? we run multiple teams and need isolation.
[23:28] Liam: Absolutely — per-route quotas, rate-limits, and per-team cost centers. The Console supports org hierarchy and quotas per org unit.

[23:55] [24:20] Maya: Okay let's recap: we'll send pilot proposal and pricing, we'll get your traces, Liam will run a quick baseline on hosted test cluster, and we'll schedule a kickoff next week. Any other asks?
[24:36] Ruth: we'll get traces to you. also, ia need to loop in infra/security for the VPC discussion.
[24:44] Maya: Great, we'll include a short infra checklist for your security team.

[25:00] [25:40] Sofia: small UX ask — can Console surface suggested schema changes (auto-suggest) from observed outputs?
[25:46] Liam: Yes, the Console has a "schema suggestions" feature in Optimize that looks at actual model outputs and suggests tightening or relaxing rules.

[26:10] [26:40] Ibrahim: anything about data residency for EU? we're in NA but have EU users.
[26:45] Maya: We can provision region-specific endpoints; for full residency, Private deployments in the region are best.

[27:10] [27:35] Ruth: we'll need a proof of concept around real network conditions — can you simulate region failovers?
[27:42] Liam: We can run fault injection in the pilot (failing primary region, observe routing). We'll log how fallback decisions are made.

[28:00] [28:20] Maya: All right, last five minutes for open Qs.
[28:24] Sofia: curious about developer experience — what's the SDK story?
[28:28] Liam: SDKs in Python/Go/JS with typed bindings for schema-driven responses so you get native objects back. There's also a CLI and DevTools plugin.

[28:50] Maya: Okay, thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the pilot doc and schedule.
[28:57] Ruth: thanks all, appreciate it.
[29:00] [call ends — note recording may have truncated some early audio] 

Notes & Annex:
- Shared links: Pilot proposal template (link: https://redwood.example/pilots/archipelago-template), Security whitepaper (link: https://redwood.example/security/attestations.pdf), Console demo recording (link: https://redwood.example/demos/archipelago-2027-08-21).
- Quick decision points: Customer target p95 < 150ms for interactive agents; strict schema enforcement with human-in-loop escalation; VPC/private option required for production.
